coverage: A full HTTP route stack was exercised while the managed scheduler used an absent runner endpoint. /healthz, /api/site, login, /api/me, /api/home, an existing report read and /api/notifications/unread stayed available through the outage checks.

A reviewed managed disable reached the stop boundary three times. The operation settled at recovery_required / managed_disable_stop_pending with one prepared stop effect and no receipt, so the unavailable endpoint was never reported as a stopped process.
The affected installation became disabled and non-openable in the app directory, and its launch route failed closed without exposing the socket path. Portal business routes remained available.

A fresh Server over the same durable state retained the same bounded operation projection and kept the business routes available. Runner unavailability is represented separately from confirmed stop; pending managed work becomes unavailable or recovery-required rather than claiming a physical stop.
Authority leases are fenced and restore pause invalidates old live authority. Readiness waits recheck revocation.
limits: The runner outage uses a local absent endpoint, and the Portal stop is a route-stack re-instantiation over the same store rather than an operating-system process kill.

This is development availability evidence across SQLite, a fresh PostgreSQL 18.6 database and race instrumentation. It is not a deployed multi-process drill, production availability claim or continuous-outage SLO.

coverage: Restart cannot reconstruct executable native handles or reclaim unknown work. Ownership, generation, writer fence and controller epoch must match the durable intent.

A second container referencing the same private mount made reference resolution ambiguous. Reconciliation refused to choose one resource, and a second daemon-client restart still found both test-owned resources unchanged.
The fixture deleted only its own two containers during teardown. Production reconciliation did not infer ownership, rewrite a resource or guess-delete the duplicate.
limits: This is development acceptance on a disposable GitHub-hosted rootful Docker worker, not a production daemon upgrade or foreign-resource cleanup claim.

The native case deliberately covers stale/orphan resources that reference the app's private mount. Resources with no reference are outside the app recovery inventory and must not be adopted or removed.

coverage: A lost start/stop acknowledgement returns uncertain with no fabricated state and no retry of the physical effect.

coverage: Object limits are checked transactionally at account, plugin and global levels; release staging rolls back on a full SQLite database; data reservation has a bounded capacity boundary.

On the disposable Linux/XFS host, the real writable fixture exhausted its 8 MiB byte limit and 128 inode limit, observed ENOSPC, retained project identity and attributes, and left a separate healthy project writable. The fixture also survived remount and detected disabled quota enforcement.
A real 16 MiB tmpfs was filled until ENOSPC, the file was removed, and a fresh write succeeded. The measured file remained at or below the kernel tmpfs bound.
An 8 MiB stderr flood against the production json-file policy (max-size 1m, max-file 2) left between 1 MiB and 3 MiB on disk, proving rotation rather than uncontrolled host growth.
Container policy fixes bounded logging and resource limits, and data writer recovery evidence is opaque and bound to the exact owner.
limits: This is a disposable GitHub-hosted Linux/Docker/XFS development drill. It is not a production volume-capacity, long-duration log soak or every-host-profile claim.
The global filesystem remained above the fixture's independent capacity floor; the evidence proves bounded refusal and cleanup, not guaranteed capacity under arbitrary host pressure.

coverage: Reinstall after a completed removal creates a new installation identity and preserves the old tombstone.
